arch.title: The Elmorians: Drinkers of Light
arch.text:
The Elmorian people lived on the sunrise face of a single great escarpment for some four thousand of their years. They had no mouths, and did not need them: an Elmorian fed by standing in light, and the green of the skin is the green of that feeding. They spoke by touch. They counted in sixes. They believed the smallest of their three eyes could see what stood behind them, and they built every door in their lives at an angle, so that nothing ever had to be turned away from.

This exhibit is arranged as an Elmorian house was: four chambers on a turning path, each opening only to a visitor who has understood the last. Please do not stack anything on the ancestors.

doors.title: Door of the Gaze
doors.text: Cut stone, one piece. The lintel carries the mark for three, repeated three times. An Elmorian door was never faced squarely; the three eyes were turned to it before it was approached, and the door itself was said to know whether it had been looked at.

doors.title: Door of the Stack
doors.text: Cut stone, one piece. The lintel carries the light glyph above a stack of four. Elmorian households kept their standing in stone rings, stacked where the morning light first landed, and a door of this kind was said to open only for a house whose stack stood in the light.

doors.title: Door of the Speech
doors.text: Cut stone, one piece. The lintel carries the touch glyph between two open tentacle marks. A visitor was expected to speak the greeting before entering, and since speech was touch, the greeting was pressed into the stones beside the door rather than said to it.

doors.title: Door of the Ancestor
doors.text: Cut stone, one piece, uncarved. The only plain door in an Elmorian house was the one that led to those who had gone to stone. It has no lock. It has never needed one: it opens when the house is arranged as the house wishes, and not before.

portrait.title: An Elmorian, in the day posture
portrait.text:
Relief on green stone. The three eyes are of three sizes, and the sizes are not decoration. The largest eye saw what was near and was called the day eye. The middle eye saw what was far. The smallest eye, set high in the brow, was said to see what stood behind, and Elmorian children were taught never to cover it while sleeping.

The single tentacle from the crown, called the sil, held water and was the organ of speech. Note the absence of a mouth: this is not damage to the relief.

drink.title: Feeding
drink.text:
An Elmorian ate nothing. The skin took what was needed from light, and an adult stood in the morning sun for the length of time it takes a shadow to cross a ring. Households were therefore built on the sunrise face of the escarpment, and the poorest houses were those the cliff shaded soonest.

A person who could not reach light was said to be going dark, which was the same word as the word for dying.

cliff.title: Houses of the sunrise face
cliff.text:
The escarpment was cut into rather than built upon. A house was a room in the rock with its opening turned east and a ledge before it, and on the ledge stood the household's light stack: stone rings, one for each generation, stacked largest at the bottom so that each ring stood in the light of the one below it.

A ring placed beneath a larger one was called a swallowed stone, and was thought to bring on the shading of the house. No stack in this hall is arranged that way. Please keep it so.

count.title: Never count alone
count.text:
Elmorians counted in sixes, and the reason is given in every telling the same way: one Elmorian sees three, and two Elmorians facing each other see six, and nothing should be counted by fewer eyes than that. Counting alone was thought to invite being counted by something in the dark that had eyes of its own.

The marks on a stem in this hall are Elmorian numerals. A stem carries up to five marks; a second stem to its right is the sixes. Visitors may find it useful to learn them.

touch.title: Speech
touch.text:
Having no mouths, Elmorians spoke by touch: the tip of one sil pressed to another in patterns of pressure that the receiving skin read as words. Speech at a distance was impossible, and so was speaking to more than one person at once. Every Elmorian conversation was private, and every crowd was silent.

Writing was the same language cut into stone, read by drawing the sil across it. The relief beside this label is meant to be touched. In this hall, it may be.

greet.title: The greeting
greet.text: A greeting of four words, pressed rather than spoken: light, eye, touch, door. Read the way Elmorian writing reads, in columns from the top and from the right. The nearest rendering is "my light is in my eye; my touch is at your door", which was said at any threshold, and said again on leaving, backwards.

gaze.title: On the turning of the eyes
gaze.text: Instructional relief. The figure turns all three eyes to the door, and the ring of marks around it counts the six positions of the eye as Elmorians counted them: from the right, and then upward. A door in an Elmorian house was approached with the eyes already on it, and the three discs on the far wall of this room were the household's practice of that courtesy.

stack.title: The rule of the stack
stack.text: Instructional relief. The sun stands over the right hand peg and the night eye over the middle. The stack is complete under the sun, largest at the bottom. At the left, a swallowed stone, struck through. A ring could be moved one at a time, and only ever onto a larger ring or onto bare stone.

six.title: The sixfold gaze
six.text:
Instructional relief, from the ancestor chamber. Two Elmorians meet, sil to sil, and their six eyes make the count that a house is measured by. Between them the relief gives the arrangement of a house at the moment of that meeting: where each eye turns, where the stack stands, and what is said. It was said that the ancestors opened their door to a house so arranged.

The curators note that the three rooms behind you can still be touched.

ancestors.title: Going to stone
ancestors.text:
An Elmorian did not die so much as darken. As the skin lost its feeding it greyed, then hardened, and the family carried the person to the innermost room of the house, where they stood among those who had gone before. The dark glyph over the third figure is the only Elmorian word that was never spoken by touch. It was only ever written.

The figure in the chamber beyond this door is not a statue.

farewell.title: The farewell
farewell.text: Stone, dark, touch, eye: "when I am stone and dark, touch my eye". Said on leaving a house, and said by the household to a person going to stone, at which point the smallest eye was touched once and then never again. Visitors who have learned the greeting will notice that the farewell is not merely its reverse.

end.title: The Ancestor
end.text:
The house is arranged, and the ancestor has opened the door. Here the exhibit ends.

The curators wish it recorded that the figure in this chamber was not carved, and that the smallest eye was already open when it was found.
